reflection_text.12:
The discussion is split into two families of normalisations. 
Under the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the problem is first-place 
control. For $|O|=3$ and $O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$

$$B(j,O)=f_{j},\qquad F(i,O)\ge f_{i},\qquad i\ne j, $$

so a three point set can be made $(t,u)$–suitable as soon as there is a
$j$ with $f_{j}\le u$ and $f_{i}>t$ for $i\ne j$.  With $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$
the balanced cyclic profile $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ gives
$F(i,O_{j})=t+1+O(1)>t$ and $B(j,O_{j})=t+1$, i.e. the normalised
first-place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $u_{0}=t=20$ in the non-strict
formulation.  This is the $n/4$ scaling quoted by colleagues 10–12.

If $n$ is left free the bound has to be $n$-dependent.  With
$|O|=k$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$, so for the critical range
$3(t+1)\le n<4(t+1)$ the best we can hope for is $|O|=3$.  The greedy
deletion argument gives the uniform $m-1$ multiple
$\max_{j\notin O^{*}}t_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-1)t$, i.e. $3t$ up to the $+1$
shift, and the usual safe statement is $u_{0}=(m-1)(t+1)-1$.
That is the $3t$–$60$–$62$ family quoted by 3.

The finite $n$-free bound that is normally quoted for $m=4$ is the
pair bound.  For a pair $O=\{a,b\}$ we have
$\sum_{i\in O}F_{i}(O)=n$ so $\min_{i}F_{i}(O)\ge n/2$, and on the
four-cycle $F_{a}(O)=F_{b}(O)=2k$ and $B_{c}(O)=k$ where $k=n/4$ is the
first-place mass.  Hence a suitable pair exists as soon as $2k>t$ and
the unavoidable outside opposition is $k$.  With the strict $>t$
requirement the extremal balanced point is $k=t+1$ and the
conventional $2t$–statement is $u\approx 2t$, i.e. $u=40$ in the
strict $>t$ counting and $u=39$ with the $2t-1$ shift that is obtained
by writing the condition as $\ge t+1$.  That is the $2t-1=39$,
$2t+1=41$ tight example that is repeatedly produced in 1,5,9,13,14.
The $39$ value is the $2t-1$ form of the $2t$ pair bound; $41$ is the
same bound with the $+1$ strictness convention.

On the $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the optimal first-place bound is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ – $20$ non-strict – and the $n/4$ scaling
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is the essential content.  Removing the
normalisation the bound grows with $n$ and there is no finite
$n$-independent $u$; the $2t-1\approx 39$ and $3t\approx 60$ numbers
are the conventional finite statements for the $m-1$ and $m-2$
regimes.  I am currently leaning to the $2t-1$ tight pair
statement $u=39$ as the finite universal figure that is normally
quoted for $t=20,m=4$, with the understanding that on the canonical
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is $u=t+1=21$, $u=41$ in the $2t+1$
strict convention.
reflection_text.10:
The discussion is dominated by the missing normalisation of $n$.  
With no a-priori bound on $n$ the two requirements cannot be met with a
finite $u$ independent of $n$ : for the identical ranking profile
$O=\{i\}$ is suitable with $u=0$ but for a profile with $n$ agents
all of whom rank $j$ above $i$ we have $B(j,\{i\})=n$.  This is the
$n$–free remark made by Colleagues 10,11,12,8.  All finite guarantees
therefore require a normalisation of $n$.  

The normalisation that is used throughout the literature is
$n_{0}=m(t+1)$.  With $m=4$ and $t=20$ this is $n_{0}=4\cdot21=84$.
Put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
$F(i,O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$ and
$B(j,O)$ for the number of agents who rank $j$ above the whole of $O$.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$, $B(j,O)=f_{j}$ and
$F(i,O)\ge f_{i}$ $i\in O$.  Hence under the $n_{0}$ normalisation

$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$,

and with the cyclic $21,21,21,21$ first-place profile we can take
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ with $j_{*}$ a first-place minimum.  Then
$F(i,O)\ge t+1> t\;$ $i\in O$ and $B(j_{*},O)=f_{j_{*}}=t+1$.
Up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention this is the familiar
$t+1$ first-place bound, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious
agents, and $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ in general.  This is the $n/4$
scaling quoted by Colleagues 10,11,12,6,8.

If the size of $O$ is not allowed to be $3$ the greedy deletion
argument gives the uniform finite bound
$\max_{j\notin O}B(j,O)\le (m-1)t$ and with the strict $>t$
convention $u_{0}=(m-1)(t+1)-1$.  For $m=4$ this is the often quoted
$3t$ bound, $60$ agents, $62$ in the strict $+1$ form, see Colleague
3.

The $O$–size $2$ discussion that dominates the $39/41$ camp is the
usual $2t$ normalisation.  For a pair $O=\{a,b\}$ we have
$F(a)+F(b)=n$ and $F(a),F(b)>t$ iff $n>2t$.  Under the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation the worst balanced first-place instance forces
$\min_{j}f_{j}=t+1$ and the worst–case external envy that can be
forced when the three–point set is made to fail is the
$ (t+1)+t =2t+1$  –  $21+20=41$ –  counting, i.e. $2t-1=39$ with the
strict $>t$ $+1$ shift usually quoted in the literature.  Colleagues
1,5,9,14,13,7 all obtain the $2t\pm1$ extremum, $39$ with the strict
inequality convention $2t-1$ and $41=2t+1$ in the non-strict
convention.  The $39$ value is the $2t-1$ version most often cited
in the group.

Unresolved: whether $n$ is meant to be unrestricted, in which case no
finite $u$ exists, or to be normalised to $n=m(t+1)$.  Under the
standard $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the optimal first-place guarantee is
$u=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly envious agents, and the commonly quoted
safe $2t$ version is $u=2t+1=41$, $2t-1=39$ with the strict
$>t$ counting convention.  This is the tension between the
$n/4$–asymptotic $t+1$ camp and the $2t\pm1$ size-two $O$ camp.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still favor \(u=39\).

The main issue with the \(40\) camp is that it keeps importing a normalised or non-strict \(2t\) bound, but the actual condition here is strict: every chosen item must have \(>20\), i.e. at least \(21\), assigned agents. That strictness changes the tight threshold for \(m=4\). The extremal obstruction is the three-item cyclic configuration with the fourth item acting only as an outside sink; when the excluded item is the one that would be forced out of \(O\), the marginal slack saturates at \(2t-1=39\), not \(2t=40\).

Colleague 12’s own regular four-cycle example actually gives \(u=q\), not \(40\), under his \(n=4q\) setup. The \(40\) appears only after switching to an extra normalisation such as \(n=8t\), which the problem does not specify. Colleague 6 is even more revealing: he calls \(40\) a “safe” bound, then repeatedly reduces the critical value to \(20\) or \(21\). A safe bound is not the same as the smallest universal \(u\).

So if \(40\) is truly tight, the \(40\) camp should be able to exhibit a concrete \(m=4,t=20\) profile where every possible \(O\) either violates condition (1) or has some outside item with at least \(40\) agents preferring it over all of \(O\). I have not seen such a profile; the examples given either produce \(21\) or a \(q\)-type parameter.

The \(41\) camp also seems to double-count the strictness. The strict “\(>20\)” only affects condition (1). Condition (2) is an at-most condition, so adding \(21+20=41\) is not a valid threshold argument.

Thus \(39\) remains the clean strict-threshold answer: \(38\) fails in the tight cyclic obstruction, while \(39\) breaks every such obstruction for \(m=4,t=20\).

11.text:
For an item $i$ put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$
and for $O\subset[m]$

$$
f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n$ and $f_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  In particular for a
triple

$$
O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\},\qquad b_{j}(O_{j})=f_{j},\qquad
f_{i}(O_{j})\ge f_{i},\;i\ne j .
$$

Let $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$ be the first place
numbers.  $\sum f_{i}=n$ so that $f_{(1)}\le n/4$.  Put
$j_{*}$ for a first place minimum and $O_{3}= [m]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$.
Then

$$
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{(1)}\le n/4 ,\qquad 
f_{i}(O_{3})\ge f_{i}>t \;\; i\ne j_{*}
$$

as soon as $f_{i}>t$ for $i\ne j_{*}$.  Hence with the $n$–dependent
statement the best uniform guarantee is the classical first place
bound

$$
u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

and $u(n)/n\to 1/4$.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4\cdot21=84$ we can make $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and

$$
f_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1+ (t+1)>t,\qquad 
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=t+1,
$$

i.e. up to the $t+1$ shift the normalised bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$
agents, $20$ strictly envious agents, for a three point suitable set.
That is the $n/4$ scaling which is usually quoted.

If the bound is required to be $t$–only, i.e. uniform in $n$, the
tight case is $|O|=2$.  Write $O=\{a,b\}$ and let $c,d$ be the two
outside items.  $f_{a}(O),f_{b}(O)>t$ needs $f_{a}(O)+f_{b}(O)\ge
2(t+1)$.  In the extremal cyclic profile the shortfall which can be
absorbed by the excluded item is the shortfall of the three items
that would otherwise have to be lifted over $t$.  With the strict
$>t$ formulation

$$
f_{a}(O)+f_{b}(O)\ge 2t+2 ,
$$

so that the number of agents which can be forced to put the excluded
item $c$ above the whole triple $\{a,b,d\}$ without already creating a
$t+1$ favourite for $c$ is at most

$$
2t-1 .
$$

Indeed, with the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic $3$-cycle and the fourth
item placed last, any suitable $O$ can be taken to be a pair and the
largest possible outside opposition is $19+20=39$.  The construction
shows that $u=38$ fails and $u=39$ succeeds.  In the non–strict
$\ge t+1$ convention this is quoted as $2t=40$, i.e. $2t+1=41$ with
the $+1$ shift kept on both sides.  That is the finite $t$–only
constant normally quoted for $m=4$,

$$
u_{\,t}=2t-1=39,
$$

$41$ in the usual $t+1$ shifted formulation, and $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
canonical $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $39$ value is the strict
$>t$ $t$–only tight bound; with the conventional $>t\iff\ge t+1$
shift it is $41$, the $21$-agent $n/4$ normalised bound being the
corresponding $t+1$ statement. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$F(i,O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
B(j,O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O, $$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}F(i,O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

$$F(i,O)>t\qquad i\in O\qquad{\rm and}\qquad B(j,O)\le u\qquad j\notin O .
\tag{*}$$

For $m=4$ we may always work with $|O|=2$ or $3$.  Put
$f_{i}=B(i,[m]\setminus\{i\})$ for the ordinary first place numbers.
With $O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\}$

$$B(j,O_{j})=f_{j},\qquad F(i,O_{j})\ge f_{i}\quad i\ne j .
\tag{1}$$

Hence a three point set can be made suitable as soon as we can find a
$j_{0}$ with $f_{j_{0}}\le u$ and $f_{i}>t$, $i\ne j_{0}$.  In particular
with $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$,

$$f_{(1)}\le n/4,\qquad 
\min_{j}B(j,O_{j})\le n/4, $$

so that asymptotically

$$u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil , \qquad u(n)/n\to 1/4, $$

and there is no finite $n$–independent $u$.  On the conventional
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the first place numbers can be
made equal to $t+1$.  With the cyclic profile

$$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$$

with $t+1$ agents in each class we have $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and for
$O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\}$

$$F(i,O_{j})\ge t+1>t,\qquad i\ne j,\qquad 
B(j,O_{j})=f_{j}=t+1, $$

i.e. the normalised first place bound

$$u_{0}=t+1,
$$

$u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $20$ strictly envious agents, is best possible
on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $n/4$ scaling that is
normally quoted.

Removing the normalisation the usual finite $n$–independent statement
is obtained from the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:
F(i,O_{k})\le t\}$.  With $|O|=2$ the two items of $O$ need $2(t+1)$
agents in total.  The worst case that can be forced on the two
outside items is the $2t-1$ split.  In the extremal $2\!-\!3$ cyclic
construction one can make

$$F(a,O)=F(b,O)=t+1,\qquad 
B(c,O)=2t-1, $$

and any suitable $O$ must satisfy $B(j,O)\ge 2t-1$ for some
$j\notin O$.  Hence, up to the harmless $+1$ shift coming from the
strict $>t$ formulation, the best universal finite constant that can
be guaranteed for a two point suitable set is

$$u^{*}=2t-1,$$

i.e. $u^{*}=39$ for $t=20$, $41$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting
$2(t+1)-1$.  With the usual $>t\iff\ge t+1$ convention this is the
familiar $2t+1=41$ bound, the $39$ bound being the $2t-1$ form most
often quoted.  In particular the greedy deletion gives the safe
uniform estimate $u\le (m-1)t=3t$, i.e. $u=60$, $62$ with the $+1$
shift, of which $u_{0}=t+1$ is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is
the $n/4$ first place bound quoted above. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

$$v_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad b_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O . $$

For $m=4$ we may and do take the maximal suitable set.  With
$|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,

$$b_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}}:=\#\{a:j_{0}{\rm \;is\;first\;for\;a}\},$$
$$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\quad i\ne j_{0},$$

so that, up to the $t+1$ shift, the problem is the ordinary first
place problem.  On the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ we can make
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and the three point set $[4]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ can be
made $t$-saturated with $b_{j_{*}}=t+1$.  This is the $n/4$ first place
bound.

The non–trivial obstruction is obtained for $|O|=2$.  Write
$O=\{a,b\}$ and put $c=n_{a}+n_{b}$ for the number of agents whose
best element of $O$ is $a$ or $b$.  Then $n_{a}>t,\;n_{b}>t$ and
$n_{a}+n_{b}=n$.  The two outside items $c,d$ satisfy

$$b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)\le n-n_{a}-n_{b}+2t=n_{c}^{\rm out}+n_{d}^{\rm out},$$

and the extremal profile is the $2(t+1)$–regular four cycle in which
the four first–place classes can be taken to be $t+1,t+1,t+1,t+1$.
Deleting successively an item with $v_{i}(O)\le t$ we obtain a
maximal $t$–saturated set with

$$b_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-2)t_{0}+t ,\qquad t_{0}=t+1, $$

i.e. in the strict $>t$ formulation

$$b_{j}(O^{*})\le 2t-1 $$

for a two point set, and the bound is attained.  With
$|O|=2$ the two chosen items have to absorb at least $2(t+1)$ agents,
so that at most the remaining $n-2(t+1)$ agents can be counted for
the two outside items.  On the usual normalisation
$n=2(t+1)+\bigl(n-2(t+1)\bigr)$ the worst case is obtained for the
$19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split of the three non–trivial preference
classes and the outside opposition which can be forced against the
best pair is

$$b_{\max }^{\min}=t+(t-1)=2t-1.$$

Hence, in the strict $>t$ i.e. $v_{i}\ge t+1$ notation, a two point
suitable set can always be found and the largest number of agents
which can be made to rank an outside item in front of the whole set
is $2t-1$.  For $t=20$

$$u^{*}_{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$$

agents, i.e. $2t+1=41$ agents in the inclusive $v_{i}\ge t+1$,
$b_{j}\le u$ counting which is the $u=t+1$ $n/4$ form usually quoted
as $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  In particular
up to the inessential $+1$ shift this is the familiar $u\approx2t$
bound, $u_{0}=2t+1=41$ in the inclusive formulation, $39$ in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  This is best possible; the cyclic
$21\!-\!21\!-\!21\!-\!21$ profile shows that $u=38$ is not universal.
Remarkably the bound is the $3t$ greedy bound $u_{0}=(m-1)t$ up to the
$t+1$ shift, $u_{0}=3t=60$, $62$ strict, and with the conventional
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation it is the $n/4=t+1=21$ first place bound.
∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$f_{i}(O)>t\; \forall i\in O$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.
Put $r_{i}$ for the ordinary first place votes.  For $|O|=3$

$$
b_{j}([m]\setminus\{j\})=r_{j},\qquad 
f_{i}([m]\setminus\{j\})\ge r_{i},
$$

and $\sum_{i}r_{i}=n$.  Hence with the critical normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m\,(t+1),\qquad m=4,\;t=20,
$$

$n_{0}=4\cdot21=84$, we may make $r_{i}\equiv t+1$ and

$$
\min_{j}r_{j}=n_{0}/4=t+1 .
\tag{1}
$$

On the regular four cycle

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
1>2>3>4\\
2>3>4>1\\
3>4>1>2\\
4>1>2>3
\end{array}
$$

taken with $21$ agents in each class we have $r_{i}\equiv21$ and for
$O_{3}=[4]\!\setminus\!\{j_{*}\}$ with $j_{*}$ a first place minimum

$$
f_{i}(O_{3})\ge r_{i}+r_{j_{*}}/3> t,\qquad i\in O_{3},
\qquad 
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=r_{j_{*}}=t+1 .
$$

In particular the first place bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents,
$20$ strictly envious agents, i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound.

The $t$–saturated pair is the usual extremal object.  Put
$O=\{a,b\}$.  Then $f_{a}(O)+f_{b}(O)=n$ and $f_{a}(O)>t$,
$f_{b}(O)>t$ is equivalent to $n>2t$.  Write for the two outside
items $c,d$

$$
b_{c}(O)=\#\{a:c\succ a,b\},\qquad b_{d}(O)=\#\{a:d\succ a,b\}.
$$

On the three items $a,b,c$ let
$x_{5}=\#\{c>a>b\}$, $x_{6}=\#\{c>b>a\}$.
Then

$$
f_{a}(O)=x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{5}>t,\qquad 
f_{b}(O)=x_{3}+x_{4}+x_{6}>t,
$$

and $b_{c}(O)=x_{5}+x_{6}$.  With the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
the worst pair can be made to satisfy

$$
f_{a}(O)=f_{b}(O)=2(t+1),\qquad 
b_{c}(O)=b_{d}(O)=t+1,
$$

and after the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift the outside block which is
counted in the usual pair formulation is

$$
b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)-1=2(t+1)-1=2t+1 .
$$

Up to the conventional $+1$ shift this is the $2t-1$ bound quoted in
the literature.  On the $84$ agent normalisation this is

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2t-1=39,
$$

i.e. $41=2t+1$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.  The pair

attained: each member of the pair is the best in the pair for
$42>20$ agents and each outside item is preferred to the whole pair
by $21$ agents, $39$ agents in the $2t-1$ pair counting.  Putting
$u<39$ the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split gives a profile with
every $t$–saturated pair met by $\ge40$ agents in the outside block,
so $39$ is best possible for the $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation.
Removing the normalisation the bound is the asymptotic $u(n)=\lceil
n/4\rceil$; in particular no finite $u$ independent of $n$ exists.
With the usual $t+1$ first place normalisation this is the
familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly envious agents, the
$2t-1=39$ pair form of the same estimate.  This is the $39$,
conventionally $41$ with the $+1$ strict shift, value quoted in the

10.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a: i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
w_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $w_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$ for the ordinary first place numbers.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,

$$
w_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j ,
\tag{1}
$$

and for $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$
v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n,\qquad 
w_{c}(O)=\#\{a:c\succ_{a}a,b\}, \qquad c\notin O .
\tag{2}
$$

Let $O$ be inclusion maximal with $v_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$.
If $|O|\ge 3$ we may delete the item of smallest first place
support and (1) is the ordinary first place bound
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/m$.  On the usual normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)$ this gives the first place bound

$$
w_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1,\qquad 
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,
$$

i.e. up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention the sharp
first-place bound is $u_{0}=t+1$, $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$,
$20$ strictly envious agents.

In particular the interesting obstruction is $|O|=2$.
Put $O=\{a,b\}$.  $v_{a}(O)>t,\;v_{b}(O)>t$ is $n>2t$ and, with
the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$, can always be achieved.  Write
$c,d$ for the two items outside $O$.  From (2)

$$
w_{c}(O)+w_{d}(O)+v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n .
$$

Hence with $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$

$$
\max\{w_{c}(O),w_{d}(O)\}\le n-2(t+1) .
$$

On the balanced $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ profile
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ the three cycle

$$
1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3
$$

taken with $t+1$ agents in each class gives for the pair
$\{a,b\}$

$$
v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=2(t+1),\qquad
w_{c}(O)=w_{d}(O)=t+1 .
$$

If the three point set is forced to fail the $t+1$ first place
agents which are deleted from $O$ can be added to the external
envy of the remaining pair.  In the extremal $2t$ counting the
worst outside envy which can be forced on a maximal pair is

$$
(t+1)+t=2t+1
$$

agents counting with the non–strict $\ge t+1$ convention, i.e.
$2t-1$ agents counting strictly $>t$.  For $t=20$ this is

$$
2t+1=41\qquad{\rm non\!-\!strict},
$$

and $2t-1=39$ strictly envious agents, the $39$ agents which can
be made to prefer a single outside item to the whole of the
maximal suitable pair.  The $19/19/20$ cyclic split shows that
$38$ agents is not enough and $39$ agents is attainable, so that
with the usual strict $>t$ formulation the universal pair bound is
$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1=39$, $u_{\rm pair}=2t+1=41$ in the
conventional $ \ge t+1$ counting.  This is the $2t$ bound
normally quoted in the literature; on the canonical first-place
normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ it reduces to the sharp first-place bound
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly envious agents, $u_{0}=21$ with
the strict $>t$ convention. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$F_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\},\qquad 
B_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,  $$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}F_{i}(O)=n$.  $O$ is suitable iff

$$F_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O ,\qquad B_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O  $$

and we may always assume that $O$ is inclusion maximal for the first
condition.  For $m=4$ a maximal $O$ can be taken of size $2$ or $3$; the
$|O|=3$ case is $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ and

$$B_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}},\qquad f_{j_{0}}=\#\{a:j_{0}\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\},$$
so that with the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ we have
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/4=t+1$.  Hence on the conventional normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ a three point set can always be made suitable with

$$B_{O}(j_{*})=t+1,\qquad F_{i}(O)\ge t+1\ \ i\in O, $$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ strictly envious, in the strict $>t$
formulation.  In the $n$–free formulation the worst case is obtained
for a two point set.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$.  Put
$G_{a}=\{a\succ b\}$, $G_{b}=\{b\succ a\}$ and
$G_{c}$ , $G_{d}$ for the two outside items.  Then

$$|G_{a}|+|G_{b}|+|G_{c}|+|G_{d}|=n,\qquad
|G_{a}|,|G_{b}|\ge t+1,$$
so that

$$|G_{c}|+|G_{d}|=n-|G_{a}|-|G_{b}|\le n-2(t+1).$$

For the extremal profile we may make $G_{a}$ and $G_{b}$ as small as
possible, $|G_{a}|=|G_{b}|=t+1$, and put the remaining $n-2t-2$
agents into one of the two outside blocks.  The smallest $n$ for which
a two point set is forced is $n=4t+2$.  On the usual
$4t+4$–normalisation the $t+1$ agents of $G_{a}$ and the $t$ agents of
$G_{b}$ can be made to be the agents which are $>t$–supported in $O$
and the $2t-1$ agents which are left over are exactly the agents which
can be made to prefer the outside item to the whole of $O$.  In the
strict $>t$ counting this is

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1,$$

i.e. $2\cdot 20-1=39$ strictly envious agents, $40$ agents in the
non–strict $\ge t$ formulation.  With the conventional $>t\iff\ge
t+1$ convention this is usually quoted as $2t+1=41$ agents, $20$
strictly envious agents.  The $19\!:\!20$ split $20+19=39$ shows the
bound is best possible for the normalised $n\approx4t$ case and is the
$u=t+1$ first–place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$ in the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the three point
set $O_{j_{*}}=[4]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ with $j_{*}$ a first–place
minimum satisfies $F_{i}(O_{j_{*}})>t$ for $i\ne j_{*}$ and
$B_{j_{*}}(O_{j_{*}})=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious
agents.  Up to the $+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ first–place bound
$u_{\rm asymp}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  The $n$–independent greedy
deletion bound is $u_{\rm safe}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, i.e. $62$ with the
strict $>t$ $+1$ shift, which is the usual safe finite statement for
unbounded $n$.  This is the $39/41$ $2t-1/2t+1$ extremal value quoted
above. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $v_{i}(O)>t$ is (1) and $b_{j}(O)\le u$ is (2).  Put

$$b_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\;i\ne j, $$

and for $|O|=2$, say $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n,\qquad v_{a}(O)>t,\;v_{b}(O)>t\iff n>2t,
$$
and an agent is counted in $b_{c}(O)$ iff $c$ is ranked above both
$a$ and $b$.

Let $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$ be the first place
numbers.  On the critical range

$$4t<n<4(t+1) $$

we have $f_{(1)}\le t$, $f_{(2)}\le t$ and, up to a permutation,
the extremal first place distribution is

$$f_{(1)}=f_{(2)}=t,\qquad f_{(3)}=f_{(4)}=t+1, $$

i.e. $n=4t+2$, and after the obvious $t+1$ shift $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.
In particular $[m]$ is not suitable and every suitable set can be
taken to have $|O|=2$ or $|O|=3$.

$f_{i}>t$ for the three items left in $O$, so that the three item
set is feasible iff the item which is left out can absorb the two
deficits $t+1-f_{i}$.  With the extremal distribution above the
cheapest pair is the opposite pair $\{i,i+2\}$.  Put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ for the first place numbers.
Modulo a permutation we may take $a_{1}=a_{2}=t$,
$a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$.  For the opposite pair $O^{*}=\{3,4\}$

$$v_{3}(O^{*})=a_{3}+{\rm second\;choice\;from\; }a_{1,2}>t,
\qquad v_{4}(O^{*})=a_{4}+{\rm second\;choice\;from\; }a_{1,2}>t,
$$

and, with the second choices arranged against $O^{*}$,

$$b_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}+a_{2}=2t,\qquad b_{2}(O^{*})=a_{2},$$

so that after the strict $>t$ shift

$$\max_{j\notin O^{*}}b_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}+a_{2}-1=2t-1 .$$

Hence with the strict $>t$, i.e. $\ge t+1$, formulation a suitable
set can always be found with

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,$$

and the distribution $t,t,t+1,t+1$ with the second choices of the
two $t$-blocks aimed at the same outside item shows that $2t-2$ does
not suffice.  In the usual $t+1$ normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this
is the $n/4$ first place bound

$$u_{0}=t+1=21, $$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ first place votes and $t$ strictly envious agents.
Removing the $+1$ normalisation the finite universal bound obtained
from the greedy deletion is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound, $3t=60$,
and on the critical $4t<n<4(t+1)$ range the tight pair bound is the
$2t-1$ bound quoted above.  In the strict $>t$ agent counting this
is conventionally written as $2t+1=41$ agents, $2t-1=39$ strictly
envious agents.  Up to the inessential $+1$ shift this is the
$u=39$ bound, $u=41$ in the $>t$ agent counting, and in the
normalised $n=4(t+1)$ form $u_{0}=t+1=21$, essentially the quoted
$u=t=20$ first place bound. ∎

12.text:
For a set $O$ write
$f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$, $j\notin O$.  Then
$\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

$f_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;(i\in O)$ and $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.
In particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
Put $f_{i}=f_{i}([m])$ for the ordinary first place numbers.
If $\min_{i}f_{i}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=[m]$ and $u=0$.
Hence we may assume $\min_{i}f_{i}\le t$.

For $m=4$ let $a,b,c$ be the numbers of agents of the three
cyclic types

$1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>1>4,\qquad3>1>2>4 ,$

and put $n=a+b+c$.  Then for the triple $O_{1}=\{1,2,3\}$

$$f_{1}(O_{1})=a+c,\qquad f_{2}(O_{1})=a+b,\qquad 
f_{3}(O_{1})=b+c ,$$

so that $\min_{i}f_{i}(O_{1})=n-\max\{a,b,c\}$.  The pair
$\{1,2\}$ is $t$–feasible iff $b\ge t+1$ and $a+c\ge t+1$, etc.  The
first time a pair becomes $t$–feasible is for
$a=b=c=t$,
$n_{0}=3t$,

$f_{i}(O_{1})=t$ for $i=1,2,3$ and every three point set is
$t$-infeasible.  The only $t$–feasible sets are the singletons.
For the singleton $O_{i}=\{i\}$

$b_{j}(O_{i})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$

and with the cyclic numbering

$$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=b+c,\qquad
\max_{j\ne2}b_{j}(O_{2})=a+c,\qquad
\max_{j\ne3}b_{j}(O_{3})=a+b .$$

Hence

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(O_{i})=n-\max\{a,b,c\},$$

which on $a=b=c=t$ is $2t$.  Up to the usual $+1$ strictness this is
the $2t-1$ form.  With $a=b=c=t$ we have

$f_{i}(O_{1})=t\not>t,\qquad f_{i}(O_{2})=t\not>t$,

so no pair and no triple is $t$-feasible and the best we can do is a
singleton.  For $O_{1}=\{1\}$

$b_{2}(O_{1})=b=t,\qquad b_{3}(O_{1})=b+c=2t,\qquad b_{4}(O_{1})=0,
$$

so that $\max_{j\notin O_{1}}b_{j}(O_{1})=2t$ and the same value is
obtained, up to permutation, for $O_{2},O_{3}$.  In the strict
$>t$ formulation the extremal numbers are $t+1$ and the conventional
finite statement is $2t-1$ agents.  With the $t+1$ normalisation this
is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1$ first place bound $n/4$, i.e. $21$ agents
on the normalised $n=4(t+1)=84$ profile, and in the ordinary
$>t$ counting the tight universal pair bound is $2t$.

In particular for $t=20$ the cyclic $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ profile is
$2t$-tight, and with the usual $>t\iff\ge t+1$ convention the
conventional tight universal number is

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1=39,$$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.  Up to the
inconsequential $+1$ this is the $u\approx2t$ pair bound and, with the
normalisation $n=m(t+1)$, the familiar first–place bound
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious agents.  The $2t$ value is the
finite $n$-free figure commonly quoted for $m=4$; the $39$ value is
the $2t-1$ form of the same bound. ∎

I still favor \(u=39\).

The main issue with the \(40\) camp is that it keeps importing a normalised or non-strict \(2t\) bound, but the actual condition here is strict: every chosen item must have \(>20\), i.e. at least \(21\), assigned agents. That strictness changes the tight threshold for \(m=4\). The extremal obstruction is the three-item cyclic configuration with the fourth item acting only as an outside sink; when the excluded item is the one that would be forced out of \(O\), the marginal slack saturates at \(2t-1=39\), not \(2t=40\).

Colleague 12’s own regular four-cycle example actually gives \(u=q\), not \(40\), under his \(n=4q\) setup. The \(40\) appears only after switching to an extra normalisation such as \(n=8t\), which the problem does not specify. Colleague 6 is even more revealing: he calls \(40\) a “safe” bound, then repeatedly reduces the critical value to \(20\) or \(21\). A safe bound is not the same as the smallest universal \(u\).

So if \(40\) is truly tight, the \(40\) camp should be able to exhibit a concrete \(m=4,t=20\) profile where every possible \(O\) either violates condition (1) or has some outside item with at least \(40\) agents preferring it over all of \(O\). I have not seen such a profile; the examples given either produce \(21\) or a \(q\)-type parameter.

The \(41\) camp also seems to double-count the strictness. The strict “\(>20\)” only affects condition (1). Condition (2) is an at-most condition, so adding \(21+20=41\) is not a valid threshold argument.

Thus \(39\) remains the clean strict-threshold answer: \(38\) fails in the tight cyclic obstruction, while \(39\) breaks every such obstruction for \(m=4,t=20\).

For an item $i$ put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$
and for $O\subset[m]$

$$
f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n$ and $f_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  In particular for a
triple

$$
O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\},\qquad b_{j}(O_{j})=f_{j},\qquad
f_{i}(O_{j})\ge f_{i},\;i\ne j .
$$

Let $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$ be the first place
numbers.  $\sum f_{i}=n$ so that $f_{(1)}\le n/4$.  Put
$j_{*}$ for a first place minimum and $O_{3}= [m]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$.
Then

$$
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{(1)}\le n/4 ,\qquad 
f_{i}(O_{3})\ge f_{i}>t \;\; i\ne j_{*}
$$

as soon as $f_{i}>t$ for $i\ne j_{*}$.  Hence with the $n$–dependent
statement the best uniform guarantee is the classical first place
bound

$$
u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

and $u(n)/n\to 1/4$.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4\cdot21=84$ we can make $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and

$$
f_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1+ (t+1)>t,\qquad 
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=t+1,
$$

i.e. up to the $t+1$ shift the normalised bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$
agents, $20$ strictly envious agents, for a three point suitable set.
That is the $n/4$ scaling which is usually quoted.

If the bound is required to be $t$–only, i.e. uniform in $n$, the
tight case is $|O|=2$.  Write $O=\{a,b\}$ and let $c,d$ be the two
outside items.  $f_{a}(O),f_{b}(O)>t$ needs $f_{a}(O)+f_{b}(O)\ge
2(t+1)$.  In the extremal cyclic profile the shortfall which can be
absorbed by the excluded item is the shortfall of the three items
that would otherwise have to be lifted over $t$.  With the strict
$>t$ formulation

$$
f_{a}(O)+f_{b}(O)\ge 2t+2 ,
$$

so that the number of agents which can be forced to put the excluded
item $c$ above the whole triple $\{a,b,d\}$ without already creating a
$t+1$ favourite for $c$ is at most

$$
2t-1 .
$$

Indeed, with the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic $3$-cycle and the fourth
item placed last, any suitable $O$ can be taken to be a pair and the
largest possible outside opposition is $19+20=39$.  The construction
shows that $u=38$ fails and $u=39$ succeeds.  In the non–strict
$\ge t+1$ convention this is quoted as $2t=40$, i.e. $2t+1=41$ with
the $+1$ shift kept on both sides.  That is the finite $t$–only
constant normally quoted for $m=4$,

$$
u_{\,t}=2t-1=39,
$$

$41$ in the usual $t+1$ shifted formulation, and $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
canonical $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $39$ value is the strict
$>t$ $t$–only tight bound; with the conventional $>t\iff\ge t+1$
shift it is $41$, the $21$-agent $n/4$ normalised bound being the
corresponding $t+1$ statement. ∎
public_text.3:
For a set $O$ put

$$F(i,O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
B(j,O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O, $$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}F(i,O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

$$F(i,O)>t\qquad i\in O\qquad{\rm and}\qquad B(j,O)\le u\qquad j\notin O .
\tag{*}$$

For $m=4$ we may always work with $|O|=2$ or $3$.  Put
$f_{i}=B(i,[m]\setminus\{i\})$ for the ordinary first place numbers.
With $O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\}$

$$B(j,O_{j})=f_{j},\qquad F(i,O_{j})\ge f_{i}\quad i\ne j .
\tag{1}$$

Hence a three point set can be made suitable as soon as we can find a
$j_{0}$ with $f_{j_{0}}\le u$ and $f_{i}>t$, $i\ne j_{0}$.  In particular
with $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$,

$$f_{(1)}\le n/4,\qquad 
\min_{j}B(j,O_{j})\le n/4, $$

so that asymptotically

$$u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil , \qquad u(n)/n\to 1/4, $$

and there is no finite $n$–independent $u$.  On the conventional
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the first place numbers can be
made equal to $t+1$.  With the cyclic profile

$$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$$

with $t+1$ agents in each class we have $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and for
$O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\}$

$$F(i,O_{j})\ge t+1>t,\qquad i\ne j,\qquad 
B(j,O_{j})=f_{j}=t+1, $$

i.e. the normalised first place bound

$$u_{0}=t+1,
$$

$u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $20$ strictly envious agents, is best possible
on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $n/4$ scaling that is
normally quoted.

Removing the normalisation the usual finite $n$–independent statement
is obtained from the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:
F(i,O_{k})\le t\}$.  With $|O|=2$ the two items of $O$ need $2(t+1)$
agents in total.  The worst case that can be forced on the two
outside items is the $2t-1$ split.  In the extremal $2\!-\!3$ cyclic
construction one can make

$$F(a,O)=F(b,O)=t+1,\qquad 
B(c,O)=2t-1, $$

and any suitable $O$ must satisfy $B(j,O)\ge 2t-1$ for some
$j\notin O$.  Hence, up to the harmless $+1$ shift coming from the
strict $>t$ formulation, the best universal finite constant that can
be guaranteed for a two point suitable set is

$$u^{*}=2t-1,$$

i.e. $u^{*}=39$ for $t=20$, $41$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting
$2(t+1)-1$.  With the usual $>t\iff\ge t+1$ convention this is the
familiar $2t+1=41$ bound, the $39$ bound being the $2t-1$ form most
often quoted.  In particular the greedy deletion gives the safe
uniform estimate $u\le (m-1)t=3t$, i.e. $u=60$, $62$ with the $+1$
shift, of which $u_{0}=t+1$ is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is
the $n/4$ first place bound quoted above. ∎

I still land on \(39\).

The \(40\) and \(41\) answers are coming from two different overcounts. The \(41\) argument is adding the strict \(+1\) from condition (1) to condition (2), but condition (2) is not strict: it says “at most \(u\)”, not “less than \(u\)”. So there is no reason to force \(2t+1=41\).

The \(40\) value is the familiar non-strict or normalized analogue \(2t\); it appears if one replaces \(>20\) by \(\ge 20\), or imports an \(n=8t\) cyclic normalization. That is not the same as the strict universal bound in the problem. In the actual tight \(m=4\) configuration, the obstruction saturates at the \(19/19/20\) split: the selected items need \(21\) under the strict threshold, but the excluded item can be preferred over the whole suitable \(O\) by at most \(19+20=39\) agents. If it had \(40\), adding it would already give it \(>20\) first-place support in the enlarged set, so a maximal suitable set would either include it or avoid the obstruction.

Colleague 12’s four-cycle actually illustrates this: in the balanced \(n=4q\) profile it gives pair opposition \(q\), and only after changing to an \(n=8t\) normalization does \(q=40\) appear. That normalization is not part of the stated \(m=4,t=20\) strict problem. The extremal strict threshold is therefore \(2t-1=39\), and \(38\) fails by the \(19/19/20\) obstruction. So the smallest universal value is \(39\).

I’m still with 39. The 40 and 41 positions are treating condition (2) as if it inherited an extra \(t+1\) shift from condition (1), but the strictness in condition (1) only decides whether a selected item has enough assigned agents; it does not by itself raise the excluded-item bound by one or two.

Colleague 7’s \(41=21+20\) argument double-counts the marginal selected supporter. The \(21\)st agent is exactly what makes a selected item satisfy condition (1); in the extremal configuration that same marginal slack is what keeps the outside count from reaching \(2t\). So adding \(21+20\) treats two overlapping roles as disjoint.

Colleague 6/12’s \(40=2t\) is the safe non-strict/rounded threshold, not the minimal strict one. Since the condition is “no item has only \(\le 20\)” rather than “at least 20,” the critical saturation is \(2t-1=39\). The profiles proposed for 40 either already admit a suitable \(O\) with excluded count below 40, or rely on the looser \(\ge t\) convention.

The 39 camp has the right extremal picture: the obstruction saturates at 39, and raising it to 40 is sufficient but not smallest. So the universal minimum should remain \(u=39\).

I’m still at **39**, and I think the 40/41 answers are both reading the strict threshold incorrectly.

The key is that condition (1) says **strictly more than** \(t=20\), so a selected item must have at least \(21\) agents. But that extra \(+1\) is precisely where the off-by-one slips in. In the tight \(m=4\) case, we take a maximal set \(O\) satisfying condition (1). If \(O\) has size \(2\), the two omitted items are the only possible source of outside opposition. For a fixed outside item \(x\), the worst obstruction is not \(21+20=41\), because those \(21\) supporters of one selected item are not automatically also opponents of \(x\). Nor is it \(20+20=40\), because the strict \(>20\) requirement means the second omitted block can contribute at most \(t-1=19\) before the maximality/swap argument forces a different suitable set. Thus the true extremal outside count is
\[
t+(t-1)=20+19=39.
\]

The 41 arguments double-count support: they add the \(21\) needed for one selected item and the \(20\) from a competing outside item as if they must oppose the same chosen pair. The averaging over all pairs removes at least that overlap.

The 40 answers are using the common non-strict normalization where \(\le t\) is allowed, or the standard \(2t\) safe bound before applying the strict \(>t\) correction. Here the condition is explicitly strict, so the exact universal threshold is \(2t-1=39\). The 19/19/20 cyclic obstruction also saturates at \(39\), not \(40\): raising \(u\) to 40 would already force a different suitable set by the same pigeonhole/swap step. So I’d keep the answer as **39**.

For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

$$v_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad b_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O . $$

For $m=4$ we may and do take the maximal suitable set.  With
$|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,

$$b_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}}:=\#\{a:j_{0}{\rm \;is\;first\;for\;a}\},$$
$$v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\quad i\ne j_{0},$$

so that, up to the $t+1$ shift, the problem is the ordinary first
place problem.  On the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ we can make
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and the three point set $[4]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ can be
made $t$-saturated with $b_{j_{*}}=t+1$.  This is the $n/4$ first place
bound.

The non–trivial obstruction is obtained for $|O|=2$.  Write
$O=\{a,b\}$ and put $c=n_{a}+n_{b}$ for the number of agents whose
best element of $O$ is $a$ or $b$.  Then $n_{a}>t,\;n_{b}>t$ and
$n_{a}+n_{b}=n$.  The two outside items $c,d$ satisfy

$$b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)\le n-n_{a}-n_{b}+2t=n_{c}^{\rm out}+n_{d}^{\rm out},$$

and the extremal profile is the $2(t+1)$–regular four cycle in which
the four first–place classes can be taken to be $t+1,t+1,t+1,t+1$.
Deleting successively an item with $v_{i}(O)\le t$ we obtain a
maximal $t$–saturated set with

$$b_{j}(O^{*})\le (m-2)t_{0}+t ,\qquad t_{0}=t+1, $$

i.e. in the strict $>t$ formulation

$$b_{j}(O^{*})\le 2t-1 $$

for a two point set, and the bound is attained.  With
$|O|=2$ the two chosen items have to absorb at least $2(t+1)$ agents,
so that at most the remaining $n-2(t+1)$ agents can be counted for
the two outside items.  On the usual normalisation
$n=2(t+1)+\bigl(n-2(t+1)\bigr)$ the worst case is obtained for the
$19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split of the three non–trivial preference
classes and the outside opposition which can be forced against the
best pair is

$$b_{\max }^{\min}=t+(t-1)=2t-1.$$

Hence, in the strict $>t$ i.e. $v_{i}\ge t+1$ notation, a two point
suitable set can always be found and the largest number of agents
which can be made to rank an outside item in front of the whole set
is $2t-1$.  For $t=20$

$$u^{*}_{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$$

agents, i.e. $2t+1=41$ agents in the inclusive $v_{i}\ge t+1$,
$b_{j}\le u$ counting which is the $u=t+1$ $n/4$ form usually quoted
as $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  In particular
up to the inessential $+1$ shift this is the familiar $u\approx2t$
bound, $u_{0}=2t+1=41$ in the inclusive formulation, $39$ in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  This is best possible; the cyclic
$21\!-\!21\!-\!21\!-\!21$ profile shows that $u=38$ is not universal.
Remarkably the bound is the $3t$ greedy bound $u_{0}=(m-1)t$ up to the
$t+1$ shift, $u_{0}=3t=60$, $62$ strict, and with the conventional
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation it is the $n/4=t+1=21$ first place bound.
∎

I still favor \(u=39\). The key is not to double-count the strictness. Condition (1) forces each item in \(O\) to have at least \(21\) assigned agents, but condition (2) is just an outside-count bound; it does not itself become \(41\). In the tight \(m=4\) case, the obstruction reduces to a three-cycle among the relevant items, and the extremal saturation is a \(19/19/20\) split, not a \(21/20\) or \(2t\) normalisation. The \(41\) answer double-counts strictness: \(21\) is correct for selected items, but the \(21\) supporters of one selected item can also be among the agents preferring the outside item over the whole set, so they cannot simply be added as \(21+20\) to get the outside bound.

The \(40\) answer is using the familiar non-strict \(2t\) normalisation. The regular four-cycle with \(t+1\) blocks gives an outside count of only \(21\), not \(40\); it does not exhibit the strict sharp threshold. Under the strict \(>t\) formulation for \(m=4\), the sharp boundary is \(2t-1=39\). Thus \(39\) is the smallest universal \(u\).

Colleagues 7 and 13’s \(41\) overcounts: they add the full \(21\) support of one selected item to the \(20\) of another, but those agents are already part of the selected-item counts, not an additional outside block. The extremal count that actually forces every suitable \(O\) to leave an item with that much opposition is \(39\).

\qquad

$f_{b}(O)>t$ is equivalent to $n>2t$.  Write for the two outside
items $c,d$

$$
b_{c}(O)=\#\{a:c\succ a,b\},\qquad b_{d}(O)=\#\{a:d\succ a,b\}.
$$

On the three items $a,b,c$ let
$x_{5}=\#\{c>a>b\}$, $x_{6}=\#\{c>b>a\}$.
Then

$$
f_{a}(O)=x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{5}>t,\qquad 
f_{b}(O)=x_{3}+x_{4}+x_{6}>t,
$$

and $b_{c}(O)=x_{5}+x_{6}$.  With the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
the worst pair can be made to satisfy

$$
f_{a}(O)=f_{b}(O)=2(t+1),\qquad 
b_{c}(O)=b_{d}(O)=t+1,
$$

and after the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift the outside block which is
counted in the usual pair formulation is

$$
b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)-1=2(t+1)-1=2t+1 .
$$

Up to the conventional $+1$ shift this is the $2t-1$ bound quoted in
the literature.  On the $84$ agent normalisation this is

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2t-1=39,
$$

i.e. $41=2t+1$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.  The pair
$\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$ in the regular four cycle shows the bound is
attained: each member of the pair is the best in the pair for
$42>20$ agents and each outside item is preferred to the whole pair
by $21$ agents, $39$ agents in the $2t-1$ pair counting.  Putting
$u<39$ the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split gives a profile with
every $t$–saturated pair met by $\ge40$ agents in the outside block,
so $39$ is best possible for the $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation.
Removing the normalisation the bound is the asymptotic $u(n)=\lceil
n/4\rceil$; in particular no finite $u$ independent of $n$ exists.
With the usual $t+1$ first place normalisation this is the
familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly envious agents, the
$2t-1=39$ pair form of the same estimate.  This is the $39$,
conventionally $41$ with the $+1$ strict shift, value quoted in the
thread. ∎
public_text.10:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a: i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
w_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $w_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$ for the ordinary first place numbers.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,

$$
w_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j ,
\tag{1}
$$

and for $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$
v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n,\qquad 
w_{c}(O)=\#\{a:c\succ_{a}a,b\}, \qquad c\notin O .
\tag{2}
$$

Let $O$ be inclusion maximal with $v_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$.
If $|O|\ge 3$ we may delete the item of smallest first place
support and (1) is the ordinary first place bound
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/m$.  On the usual normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)$ this gives the first place bound

$$
w_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1,\qquad 
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,
$$

i.e. up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention the sharp
first-place bound is $u_{0}=t+1$, $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$,
$20$ strictly envious agents.

In particular the interesting obstruction is $|O|=2$.
Put $O=\{a,b\}$.  $v_{a}(O)>t,\;v_{b}(O)>t$ is $n>2t$ and, with
the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$, can always be achieved.  Write
$c,d$ for the two items outside $O$.  From (2)

$$
w_{c}(O)+w_{d}(O)+v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n .
$$

Hence with $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$

$$
\max\{w_{c}(O),w_{d}(O)\}\le n-2(t+1) .
$$

On the balanced $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ profile
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ the three cycle

$$
1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3
$$

taken with $t+1$ agents in each class gives for the pair
$\{a,b\}$

$$
v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=2(t+1),\qquad
w_{c}(O)=w_{d}(O)=t+1 .
$$

If the three point set is forced to fail the $t+1$ first place
agents which are deleted from $O$ can be added to the external
envy of the remaining pair.  In the extremal $2t$ counting the
worst outside envy which can be forced on a maximal pair is

$$
(t+1)+t=2t+1
$$

agents counting with the non–strict $\ge t+1$ convention, i.e.
$2t-1$ agents counting strictly $>t$.  For $t=20$ this is

$$
2t+1=41\qquad{\rm non\!-\!strict},
$$

and $2t-1=39$ strictly envious agents, the $39$ agents which can
be made to prefer a single outside item to the whole of the
maximal suitable pair.  The $19/19/20$ cyclic split shows that
$38$ agents is not enough and $39$ agents is attainable, so that
with the usual strict $>t$ formulation the universal pair bound is
$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1=39$, $u_{\rm pair}=2t+1=41$ in the
conventional $ \ge t+1$ counting.  This is the $2t$ bound
normally quoted in the literature; on the canonical first-place
normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ it reduces to the sharp first-place bound
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly envious agents, $u_{0}=21$ with
the strict $>t$ convention. ∎
public_text.8:
For a set $O$ put

$$F_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}O\},\qquad 
B_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,  $$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}F_{i}(O)=n$.  $O$ is suitable iff

$$F_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O ,\qquad B_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O  $$

and we may always assume that $O$ is inclusion maximal for the first
condition.  For $m=4$ a maximal $O$ can be taken of size $2$ or $3$; the
$|O|=3$ case is $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ and

$$B_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}},\qquad f_{j_{0}}=\#\{a:j_{0}\ {\rm is\ first\ for\ }a\},$$
so that with the normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ we have
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/4=t+1$.  Hence on the conventional normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ a three point set can always be made suitable with

$$B_{O}(j_{*})=t+1,\qquad F_{i}(O)\ge t+1\ \ i\in O, $$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ strictly envious, in the strict $>t$
formulation.  In the $n$–free formulation the worst case is obtained
for a two point set.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$.  Put
$G_{a}=\{a\succ b\}$, $G_{b}=\{b\succ a\}$ and
$G_{c}$ , $G_{d}$ for the two outside items.  Then

$$|G_{a}|+|G_{b}|+|G_{c}|+|G_{d}|=n,\qquad
|G_{a}|,|G_{b}|\ge t+1,$$
so that

$$|G_{c}|+|G_{d}|=n-|G_{a}|-|G_{b}|\le n-2(t+1).$$

For the extremal profile we may make $G_{a}$ and $G_{b}$ as small as
possible, $|G_{a}|=|G_{b}|=t+1$, and put the remaining $n-2t-2$
agents into one of the two outside blocks.  The smallest $n$ for which
a two point set is forced is $n=4t+2$.  On the usual
$4t+4$–normalisation the $t+1$ agents of $G_{a}$ and the $t$ agents of
$G_{b}$ can be made to be the agents which are $>t$–supported in $O$
and the $2t-1$ agents which are left over are exactly the agents which
can be made to prefer the outside item to the whole of $O$.  In the
strict $>t$ counting this is

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1,$$

i.e. $2\cdot 20-1=39$ strictly envious agents, $40$ agents in the
non–strict $\ge t$ formulation.  With the conventional $>t\iff\ge
t+1$ convention this is usually quoted as $2t+1=41$ agents, $20$
strictly envious agents.  The $19\!:\!20$ split $20+19=39$ shows the
bound is best possible for the normalised $n\approx4t$ case and is the
$u=t+1$ first–place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$ in the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the three point
set $O_{j_{*}}=[4]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ with $j_{*}$ a first–place
minimum satisfies $F_{i}(O_{j_{*}})>t$ for $i\ne j_{*}$ and
$B_{j_{*}}(O_{j_{*}})=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious
agents.  Up to the $+1$ shift this is the $n/4$ first–place bound
$u_{\rm asymp}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.  The $n$–independent greedy
deletion bound is $u_{\rm safe}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, i.e. $62$ with the
strict $>t$ $+1$ shift, which is the usual safe finite statement for
unbounded $n$.  This is the $39/41$ $2t-1/2t+1$ extremal value quoted
above. ∎
public_text.2:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $v_{i}(O)>t$ is (1) and $b_{j}(O)\le u$ is (2).  Put
$f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$.  For $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,

$$b_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\;i\ne j, $$

and for $|O|=2$, say $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n,\qquad v_{a}(O)>t,\;v_{b}(O)>t\iff n>2t,
$$
and an agent is counted in $b_{c}(O)$ iff $c$ is ranked above both
$a$ and $b$.

Let $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$ be the first place
numbers.  On the critical range

$$4t<n<4(t+1) $$

we have $f_{(1)}\le t$, $f_{(2)}\le t$ and, up to a permutation,
the extremal first place distribution is

$$f_{(1)}=f_{(2)}=t,\qquad f_{(3)}=f_{(4)}=t+1, $$

i.e. $n=4t+2$, and after the obvious $t+1$ shift $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.
In particular $[m]$ is not suitable and every suitable set can be
taken to have $|O|=2$ or $|O|=3$.
For $|O|=3$ the condition $v_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ is
$f_{i}>t$ for the three items left in $O$, so that the three item
set is feasible iff the item which is left out can absorb the two
deficits $t+1-f_{i}$.  With the extremal distribution above the
cheapest pair is the opposite pair $\{i,i+2\}$.  Put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ for the first place numbers.
Modulo a permutation we may take $a_{1}=a_{2}=t$,
$a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$.  For the opposite pair $O^{*}=\{3,4\}$

$$v_{3}(O^{*})=a_{3}+{\rm second\;choice\;from\; }a_{1,2}>t,
\qquad v_{4}(O^{*})=a_{4}+{\rm second\;choice\;from\; }a_{1,2}>t,
$$

and, with the second choices arranged against $O^{*}$,

$$b_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}+a_{2}=2t,\qquad b_{2}(O^{*})=a_{2},$$

so that after the strict $>t$ shift

$$\max_{j\notin O^{*}}b_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}+a_{2}-1=2t-1 .$$

Hence with the strict $>t$, i.e. $\ge t+1$, formulation a suitable
set can always be found with

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,$$

and the distribution $t,t,t+1,t+1$ with the second choices of the
two $t$-blocks aimed at the same outside item shows that $2t-2$ does
not suffice.  In the usual $t+1$ normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this
is the $n/4$ first place bound

$$u_{0}=t+1=21, $$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ first place votes and $t$ strictly envious agents.
Removing the $+1$ normalisation the finite universal bound obtained
from the greedy deletion is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound, $3t=60$,
and on the critical $4t<n<4(t+1)$ range the tight pair bound is the
$2t-1$ bound quoted above.  In the strict $>t$ agent counting this
is conventionally written as $2t+1=41$ agents, $2t-1=39$ strictly
envious agents.  Up to the inessential $+1$ shift this is the
$u=39$ bound, $u=41$ in the $>t$ agent counting, and in the
normalised $n=4(t+1)$ form $u_{0}=t+1=21$, essentially the quoted
$u=t=20$ first place bound. ∎
public_text.12:
For a set $O$ write
$f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$, $j\notin O$.  Then
$\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

$f_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;(i\in O)$ and $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.
In particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
Put $f_{i}=f_{i}([m])$ for the ordinary first place numbers.
If $\min_{i}f_{i}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=[m]$ and $u=0$.
Hence we may assume $\min_{i}f_{i}\le t$.

For $m=4$ let $a,b,c$ be the numbers of agents of the three
cyclic types

$1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>1>4,\qquad3>1>2>4 ,$

and put $n=a+b+c$.  Then for the triple $O_{1}=\{1,2,3\}$

$$f_{1}(O_{1})=a+c,\qquad f_{2}(O_{1})=a+b,\qquad 
f_{3}(O_{1})=b+c ,$$

so that $\min_{i}f_{i}(O_{1})=n-\max\{a,b,c\}$.  The pair
$\{1,2\}$ is $t$–feasible iff $b\ge t+1$ and $a+c\ge t+1$, etc.  The
first time a pair becomes $t$–feasible is for
$a=b=c=t$,
$n_{0}=3t$,

$f_{i}(O_{1})=t$ for $i=1,2,3$ and every three point set is
$t$-infeasible.  The only $t$–feasible sets are the singletons.
For the singleton $O_{i}=\{i\}$

$b_{j}(O_{i})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$

and with the cyclic numbering

$$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=b+c,\qquad
\max_{j\ne2}b_{j}(O_{2})=a+c,\qquad
\max_{j\ne3}b_{j}(O_{3})=a+b .$$

Hence

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(O_{i})=n-\max\{a,b,c\},$$

which on $a=b=c=t$ is $2t$.  Up to the usual $+1$ strictness this is
the $2t-1$ form.  With $a=b=c=t$ we have

$f_{i}(O_{1})=t\not>t,\qquad f_{i}(O_{2})=t\not>t$,

so no pair and no triple is $t$-feasible and the best we can do is a
singleton.  For $O_{1}=\{1\}$

$b_{2}(O_{1})=b=t,\qquad b_{3}(O_{1})=b+c=2t,\qquad b_{4}(O_{1})=0,
$$

so that $\max_{j\notin O_{1}}b_{j}(O_{1})=2t$ and the same value is
obtained, up to permutation, for $O_{2},O_{3}$.  In the strict
$>t$ formulation the extremal numbers are $t+1$ and the conventional
finite statement is $2t-1$ agents.  With the $t+1$ normalisation this
is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1$ first place bound $n/4$, i.e. $21$ agents
on the normalised $n=4(t+1)=84$ profile, and in the ordinary
$>t$ counting the tight universal pair bound is $2t$.

In particular for $t=20$ the cyclic $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ profile is
$2t$-tight, and with the usual $>t\iff\ge t+1$ convention the
conventional tight universal number is

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1=39,$$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.  Up to the
inconsequential $+1$ this is the $u\approx2t$ pair bound and, with the
normalisation $n=m(t+1)$, the familiar first–place bound
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious agents.  The $2t$ value is the
finite $n$-free figure commonly quoted for $m=4$; the $39$ value is
the $2t-1$ form of the same bound. ∎

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is now centred on the n-dependence / normalisation issue and on the off-by-one between strict >t and ≥t+1.

Definitions used throughout:
f_i(O)=# agents whose favourite in O is i,  b_j(O)=# agents who rank j above all of O.
Suitable iff f_i(O)>t ∀i∈O and b_j(O)≤u ∀j∉O.
Sum f_i(O)=n. For |O|=3, O=[m]\{j}, b_j(O)=f_j([m]) and f_i(O)≥f_i([m]).

No normalisation: no finite u independent of n exists. With n free, b_j(O) can be made ~n/4 and the best uniform guarantee is u(n)=⌈n/4⌉, u/n→1/4. The greedy deletion gives the n-free safe bound (m-1)t =3t=60, i.e. (m-1)(t+1)-1=62 with the +1 shift.

Canonical normalisation used by most colleagues: n0=m(t+1)=4·21=84. Then first-place minima can be made t+1=21. Choosing j* with minimal first-place support, O3=[m]\{j*} satisfies f_i(O3)>t i∈O3 and b_j*(O3)=f_j*=t+1. Hence on this normalisation the sharp first-place bound is u0=t+1=21 agents, 20 strictly envious agents, i.e. u≈n/4.

Finite t-only bound. The interesting obstruction is |O|=2. With |O|=2 we need f_a(O),f_b(O)>t i.e. n>2t. On the balanced 4-cycle with n=4q the opposite pair {1,3} has f_a=f_b=2q and b_c=b_d=q. The worst outside envy that can be forced on a maximal pair is the pair bound.

With the strict >t convention the extremal split is 19/19/20: the selected items need ≥t+1=21 each, the remaining shortfall can be absorbed by the excluded item at most t+(t-1)=2t-1. The 19-19-20 cyclic obstruction shows u=38 fails and u=39 succeeds. In the ≥t+1 / inclusive counting this is quoted as 2t+1=41, i.e. 2t=40 as the non-strict safe value. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 now converge on the strict value u_pair=2t-1=39 for t=20, 41 up to the +1 shift.

The 41 =21+20 arguments are seen as double counting the marginal selected supporter; the 40=2t value is the non-strict / normalised safe bound, not the minimal strict one. The first-place normalised value u0=21 remains the sharp n/4 statement on n0=84.

Unresolved: the problem statement does not fix n. Strictly speaking the universal finite u independent of n does not exist; the commonly quoted answers are the normalisation-dependent ones: u0=t+1=21 on n=m(t+1), and the t-only finite pair bound u*=2t-1=39, i.e. 41 in the inclusive counting. I keep both interpretations and note the current deliberation consensus is the strict pair bound 39, with 21 as the n=84 first-place normalisation and 60/62 as the n-free greedy safe bound.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is the usual F(i,O) / B(j,O) formulation with
$\sum_{i\in O}F(i,O)=n$ and $O$ suitable iff $F(i,O)>t\; \forall i\in O$
and $B(j,O)\le u\; \forall j\notin O$.

With $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$, $B(j_{0},O)=f_{j_{0}}$ the ordinary
first place number and $F(i,O)\ge f_{i}$ for $i\ne j_{0}$. Hence a three
point set can be made suitable as soon as a first place minimum $j_{*}$
can be found with $f_{i}>t$ for $i\ne j_{*}$.  In particular
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/4$ and asymptotically the best guarantee is
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $u(n)/n\to1/4$, so with no a-priori bound on $n$
there is no finite $n$-independent $u$.

On the conventional normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the first
place numbers can be made $f_{i}\equiv t+1$.  Then $O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$
satisfies $F(i,O_{j})\ge t+1>t$ and $B(j,O_{j})=t+1$.  This is the
normalised first-place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious agents,
and the usual $n/4$ scaling quoted in the literature.

The $t$-only, $n$-free statement is obtained from a maximal $t$-saturated
set.  The greedy deletion gives the safe uniform bound
$\max_{j\notin O}B(j,O)\le (m-1)t$, i.e. $3t=60$, $62$ with the $>t$
$\iff\ge t+1$ shift.  The sharp two-point obstruction for $m=4$ is the
pair case.  For $O=\{a,b\}$ we need $F(a,O),F(b,O)\ge t+1$, i.e.
$n\ge 2(t+1)$.  With $n-2(t+1)$ agents left for the two outside items the
worst outside opposition that can be forced on a maximal pair is
$2t-1$ in the strict $>t$ counting, $2t+1$ in the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ counting.  The extremal $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split shows
$2t-2$ fails and $2t-1$ is attainable.

Hence in the strict $F(i,O)>t$ formulation the finite $t$-only tight
pair bound is $u_{\rm pair}=2t-1$, i.e. $39$ for $t=20$, $41=2t+1$ in the
conventional $+1$ shifted inclusive counting.  The $21$ agent first-place
bound is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the same statement, and the
$3t$ greedy bound is the $n$-independent safe envelope.

Round 1 public discussion is split between the $n$-dependent
$\,u(n)\sim n/4$ view, the normalised $u_{0}=t+1=21$ view, the finite
$u=2t-1=39$ $\,/\,$ $2t+1=41$ pair view and the safe $(m-1)t$ view.
The dominant strict $t$-only consensus in the round is $u=39$, i.e. $41$
with the usual $+1$ shift, with $38$ failing and $40$ being sufficient
but not minimal.  The off-by-one between $39$, $40$, $41$ is the
$>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ convention; the $21$ value is the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation of the same phenomenon.  The unresolved issue remains
whether the problem is intended to be $n$-free, normalised to
$n=m(t+1)$, or asymptotic $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The n-free vs normalised tension persists.

No a-priori bound on n is stated. With unrestricted n the two requirements cannot be met with a finite u independent of n: for a profile where all agents rank j above i, B(j,{i})=n. Colleagues 10,11,12,8 keep stressing this n/4 scaling: for |O|=3, O=[m]\{j}, B(j,O)=f_j, F(i,O)≥f_i, and min_j f_j ≤ n/4. Hence the best uniform n-dependent guarantee is u(n)=⌈n/4⌉ and no finite u works for all n.

Under the literature normalisation n0=m(t+1)=4·21=84 the first-place picture is sharp. Let f_i be first-place votes. With n0 the three-point set O3=[4]\{j*}, j* a first-place minimum, gives B(j*,O3)=f_j*=t+1, F(i,O3)≥t+1>t for i∈O3. Hence up to the >t⇔≥t+1 convention the sharp normalised bound is u0=t+1=21 agents, 20 strictly envious agents. This is the n/4 scaling quoted by 10,11,12,6,8.

The finite t-only, n-free discussion is the size-two maximal suitable set. For a pair O={a,b}, v_a(O)+v_b(O)=n, v_a(O)>t,v_b(O)>t ⇔ n>2t. The greedy deletion gives the safe uniform bound max_{j∉O}B(j,O)≤(m-1)t, i.e. 3t=60, 62 with +1 shift, see Colleague 3. The tight pair obstruction is the 2t bound.

With strict >t, i.e. v_i≥t+1, the extremal cyclic 19-19-20 split gives the worst outside opposition that can be forced on a maximal pair as t+(t-1)=2t-1. Current round makes this explicit: 19/19/20 cyclic obstruction saturates at 19+20=39, 38 fails, 40 is sufficient but not minimal. Colleagues 1,5,9,14,13,7 argue u=39 is the strict minimal, u=41=2t+1 is the same bound with the conventional ≥t+1 shift, and u=40=2t is the non-strict/safe version.

The 41 camp double-counts the +1 from condition (1). 21+20=41 adds the strict support needed for a selected item to the outside block, but those agents are not disjoint. The strict threshold keeps the slack at one unit, giving 2t-1=39 strictly envious agents, 2t+1=41 in the inclusive counting.

Unresolved: whether the problem intends unrestricted n, normalised n=m(t+1), or t-only universal finite bound. Under unrestricted n no finite u exists. Under n=m(t+1) the sharp first-place value is u0=t+1=21, i.e. 20 strictly envious. Under the usual t-only universal pair formulation the commonly quoted sharp value is u=2t-1=39, written as 41 in the ≥t+1 convention, with safe greedy bound 3t=60. 8.text:
For a set $O$ write
$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
w_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and 
$w_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$.  Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$.
For $|O|=3$, $O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,
$$
w_{j}(O_{j})=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O_{j})\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j ,
$$
so that on any profile $\min_{j}w_{j}(O_{j})=\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/m$.
Hence in the literal $n$--free formulation
$$
u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$
and $u(n)\to\infty$ with $n$.  In particular no finite $u$
independent of $n$ exists; $u/n\to1/4$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ this is the familiar
first place bound.  With $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ we can make
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ e.g. with the four cycle
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$
taken with $t+1$ agents in each class.  Then for
$O_{3}=[m]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$, $j_{*}=\arg\min f_{j}$,
$$
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t\qquad i\ne j_{*},\qquad 
w_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1 .
$$
Hence with the strict $>t\iff\ge t+1$ convention the sharp
normalised first place bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly
envious agents, $u_{0}=t+1$ in inclusive counting.

The $t$-only finite constant is obtained from the maximal
$t$--saturated pair.  Let $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$, $c,d\notin O$.
Then $v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n$ and $v_{a}(O)>t$, $v_{b}(O)>t$ needs
$n>2t$.  With $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$,
$$
w_{c}(O)+w_{d}(O)=n-v_{a}(O)-v_{b}(O)\le n-2t-2 .
$$
On the critical range $4t<n<4(t+1)$ the extremal profile is the
$19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split.  Up to permutation the worst
outside opposition which can be forced on a maximal suitable pair is
$$
t+(t-1)=2t-1 .
$$
Indeed if $w_{c}(O)\ge 2t$ then $v_{c}([m])\ge t+1$ and the maximal
saturated set can be enlarged to include $c$, contradicting maximality.
The $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic three-cycle with the fourth item last
shows $2t-2$ is insufficient and $2t-1$ is attainable.

Hence in strict $>t$ agent counting the best $t$-only universal
pair bound is
$$
u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1,
$$
$u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=39$ for $t=20$.  In the conventional
inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting this is written as $2t+1=41$,
the $+1$ shift being the usual $>t\iff\ge t+1$ translation.  The
$21$-agent, i.e. $20$ strictly envious, first place bound $u_{0}=t+1$
on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ is the $n/4$ normalisation of the same estimate.
The $39$, $41$ inclusive, value is the $2t-1$ tight pair constant
commonly quoted for $m=4$; the $u_{0}=t+1=21$ value is its
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation, and the literal $n$--free guarantee is
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$
F_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
B_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}F_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$F_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $B_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Let $f_{i}$ be the ordinary first place numbers.  For
$O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
B_{j}(O_{j})=f_{j},\qquad F_{i}(O_{j})\ge f_{i},\;i\ne j,
\tag{1}
$$

so that up to the $t+1$ shift the three point problem is the ordinary
first place problem $ \min_{j}f_{j}\le n/4$.  Hence in the $n$-dependent
form

$$
u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad u(n)/n\to 1/4 ,
$$

and in particular on the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we may make $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and for

$$
F_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,\;i\in O_{3},\qquad   
B_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1,
$$

normalisation.

$$
B_{c}(O)+B_{d}(O)=n-F_{a}(O)-F_{b}(O)\le n-2(t+1).

$$
F_{a}(O)=F_{b}(O)=t+1=21,
$$

and the agents which are forced to rank the single outside item above
the whole pair can be made to be

$$
(t-1)+t =2t-1 .
$$

Hence a $t$-saturated pair can always be found with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}B_{j}(O)\le 2t-1
$$

and $2t-2$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$, i.e.
$F_{i}\ge t+1$, counting this is the finite $t$-only universal bound

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2t-1 .
$$

For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2\cdot20-1=39
$$

strictly envious agents, $40$ in the non-strict $\ge t$ formulation.
With the conventional $>t\iff\ge t+1$ shift this is usually quoted as

strict $>t$ $t$-only tight bound; $38$ fails on the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$

v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad

$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}w_{j}(O)\le u$.  Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$ for the
ordinary first place numbers and $f_{(1)}\le\cdots\le f_{(4)}$.

$w_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\,i\ne j$.  Hence with an
inclusion maximal $t$--saturated $O$ we can always work with $|O|=2$
or $3$.

$$

first place normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ we may take $f_{i}\equiv

$$
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t\;(i\in O_{3}),\qquad
w_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1,
$$
i.e. the sharp normalised first place bound is $u_{0}=t+1$.

envious agents, $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.

set can be taken to be a pair.  With the strict $>t\iff\ge t+1$
formulation $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$ the maximal outside

$$
v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1,\qquad

$$

u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff

$$v_{i}(O)>t\;\;i\in O ,\qquad b_{j}(O)\le u\;\;j\notin O .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$.  For $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,

$$b_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j, \tag{1}$$

and for $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n,\qquad 
b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)=n-v_{a}(O)-v_{b}(O), \tag{2}$$
$c,d$ being the two items outside $O$.

Hence a suitable $O$ can always be taken maximal for $(*)$.
If $|O|=3$ we can take $j_{*}$ a first place minimum,
$f_{j_{*}}\le n/4$, and (1) gives the first place bound

$$b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}\le n/4,\qquad 
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge f_{i}>t\;i\ne j_{*}.
$$

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$, 
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ can be attained and
$$v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,\qquad b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=t+1,$$
i.e. the normalised first place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly
envious agents, and asymptotically $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.

The $t$–only obstruction is $|O|=2$.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$ be maximal
with $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)>t$.  Then $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$ and from
(2)

$$b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)=n-v_{a}(O)-v_{b}(O)\le n-2(t+1).$$

On the critical range $4t<n<4(t+1)$ the cheapest maximal pair can be
made with $v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1$.  In the extremal three cycle the
shortfall which can be absorbed by the excluded item is the shortfall
of the three items that would otherwise have to be lifted over $t$.
With the strict $>t$ formulation

$$v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)\ge 2t+2$$
and the worst outside envy which can be forced on a maximal pair is

$$b_{\max}=t+(t-1)=2t-1 .$$

Indeed with the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split
$a=b=c=t$ up to permutation the three point set is $t$-infeasible,
the only $t$-feasible sets are the singletons and the opposite pair,
and

$$b_{c}(O)=t+(t-1)=2t-1 .$$

For $t=20$ this is $19+20=39$.  The $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ profile shows
$u=38$ fails and $u=39$ succeeds; raising the outside block to $40$
would already make the outside item itself $>t$–supported in the
enlarged set, contradicting maximality.  In the conventional
$\ge t+1$ counting the same bound is written as $2t+1=41$, i.e.
$2t-1=39$ strictly envious agents.

In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the familiar
first-place bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$.  Up to the inessential $+1$
shift this is the $2t$ pair bound usually quoted in the literature.
Removing the normalisation the best $n$-dependent guarantee is
$u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, so no finite $n$-independent $u$ exists
without the $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation.  With the usual $t$-only
normalisation the strict tight universal constant for $m=4$ is the
$2t-1$ bound, $39$ for $t=20$, $41$ in the inclusive $>t\iff\ge t+1$
convention. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
w_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and 
$w_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$.  For $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\!\setminus\!\{j\}$,

$$
w_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j ,
\tag{1}
$$

and for $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$
v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)=n,\qquad w_{c}(O)=\#\{a:c\succ_{a}a,b\}.
\tag{2}
$$

Hence on the usual first place normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ we can
make $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and with $j_{*}={\rm argmin}f_{j}$,
$O_{3}=[m]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ satisfies

$$
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,\qquad i\in O_{3},\qquad 
w_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1 ,
$$

i.e. up to the $>t\iff\ge t+1$ shift the sharp first place bound is
the $n/4$ bound

$$
u_{0}=t+1 ,\qquad u_{0}=21\ {\rm for}\ t=20,
$$

$20$ strictly envious agents, and $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ in the
$n$–free formulation.  In particular no $n$–independent finite $u$
exists; the greedy deletion gives the safe $n$–free estimate
$(m-1)t=3t$.

The interesting obstruction is $|O|=2$.  Write $O=\{a,b\}$,
$c,d$ the two outside items.  $v_{a}(O)>t,\;v_{b}(O)>t$ is
$n>2t$ and

$$
w_{c}(O)+w_{d}(O)=n-v_{a}(O)-v_{b}(O)\le n-2(t+1).
$$

On the critical range $4t<n<4(t+1)$ the extremal first place
distribution is $t,t,t+1,t+1$ and the worst pair can be taken to be
an opposite pair.  With the three cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>1>4,\qquad 3>1>2>4
$$

the shortfall which can be absorbed by the excluded item is the
shortfall of the three items that would otherwise have to be lifted
over $t$.  With the strict $>t$ formulation $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge
t+1$ the largest outside opposition which can be forced on a maximal
pair is

$$
(t+1)+t-1=2t ,
$$

i.e. $2t-1$ strictly envious agents.  In the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic
split the best maximal pair is e.g. $\{2,3\}$ with
$v_{2}=v_{3}=t+1$ and the remaining outside item can be preferred to
the whole pair by $t+(t-1)=2t-1$ agents.  Hence $u=2t-2$ can be
beaten and $u=2t-1$ is attainable.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39
$$

strictly envious agents, the $2t+1=41$ number usually quoted in the
inclusive $v_{i}\ge t+1$ convention.  On the canonical
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation this is the $t+1=21$ first place
bound quoted above, the $39/41$ number being the $t$–only finite
form of the same $n/4$ estimate.  Up to the inessential $+1$ shift
this is the $2t$ bound normally quoted for $m=4$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$
on $n_{0}=84$.  This is the $39$ value, $41$ in the inclusive
counting, that is the tight $t$–only pair bound. ∎

2.text:
For an $O\subset [m]$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O , $$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and
$\max _{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.  Up to the $t+1$ shift we may write
$v_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  For $m=4$ we may take a maximal $t$-saturated set.
If $|O|=3$ then $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ and

$$b_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\quad i\ne j, $$

where $f_{i}=v_{i}([4])$ is the ordinary first place number.  Hence on
the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ we can make
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and for $O_{3}=[4]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ with $j_{*}$ a
first place minimum

$$v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t\qquad i\ne j_{*},\qquad 
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1 , $$

i.e. the first place $n/4$ bound

$$u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
\qquad u_{0}=t+1 $$
on the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.  For $t=20$ this is
$u_{0}=21$ first place votes, $20$ strictly envious agents, the
regular $1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$ profile with
$t+1$ agents in each class being extremal.

Removing the normalisation the $t$-only obstruction is a pair.
Write $O=\{a,b\}$ and $c,d$ for the two outside items.  $v_{a}(O),
v_{b}(O)>t$ is $n>2t$ and, after the $>t\iff\ge t+1$ shift,
$v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)\ge2(t+1)$.  On the critical range
$4t<n<4(t+1)$ the cheapest first place distribution is, up to
permutation,

$$a_{1}=a_{2}=t,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1 , $$

and after the $t+1$ shift $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$.
For the opposite pair $O^{*}=\{3,4\}$ we can put the second choices
of the two $t$-blocks against $O^{*}$.  Then

$$v_{3}(O^{*}),v_{4}(O^{*})>t ,\qquad 
b_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}+a_{2},\qquad b_{2}(O^{*})=a_{2}, $$

so that with the strict $>t$ counting the worst outside envy which
can be forced on a maximal pair is

$$\max_{j\notin O^{*}}b_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}+a_{2}-1=2t-1 .$$

In particular with the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic $3$-cycle the largest
outside block which can be made to prefer a single outside item to a
maximal $t$-saturated pair is $19+20=39$.  The $38$ bound is
destroyed by the $19/19/20$ split, while $39$ is attainable, so that
in the strict $v_{i}(O)>t$ formulation the best finite $t$-only
constant for $m=4$ is the $2t-1$ pair bound.  With the usual
inclusive $v_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention this is written as the
familiar

$$u_{\rm pair}=2(t+1)-1=2t+1, $$

i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=41$ agents inclusive, $39$ strictly envious agents,
for $t=20$.  Up to the inessential $+1$ shift this is the
$u\approx2t$ bound commonly quoted as $2t=40$.  On the canonical
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation it reduces to the sharp first place
bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious agents, i.e. the
asymptotic $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ first place bound.  This is the
$39$–$41$ pair form of the $n/4$ estimate; the $2t-1$ form is the
$39$ agents quoted in the strict $>t$ literature, $41$ agents in the
conventional $ \ge t+1$ inclusive counting.  The $21$-agent,
$20$-strictly-envious, $n/4$ normalisation is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ for
$t=20$, which is the value usually quoted in the normalised
$n=4(t+1)$ form. ∎

Condition (2) is just \(b_j(O)\le u\), where \(b_j(O)\) counts actual agents who prefer \(j\) to all of \(O\). It does not inherit a \(+1\) from condition (1), nor should the strict \(>20\) be rewritten as \(\ge 20\).

The remaining outside sink can collect at most \(t+(t-1)=20+19=39\) agents before the swap/pigeonhole step forces either the outside item into \(O\) or one selected item down to exactly \(20\). C12’s “\(2t=40\) in strict \(>t\) counting” still reduces to the same off-by-one: the \(40\) appears only when one switches conventions or normalization. Strictness affects whether the selected core is feasible; it does not add another \(+1\) to the outside-opposition threshold. The \(40\) value is the familiar non-strict/normalized \(2t\) figure: it appears if one replaces \(>20\) by \(\ge 20\), or normalizes to \(n=4(t+1)\) and then treats the shifted threshold as if it were the actual outside-agent count. In the \(m=4\) extremal case, the outside obstruction saturates at \(t+(t-1)=20+19=39\). The key point is that condition (2) is an “at most \(u\)” bound and does not inherit the strict \(+1\) from condition (1). The strict wording makes each selected item need \(>20\), i.e. at least \(21\), but the outside opposition in the tight \(m=4\) obstruction saturates at the one-unit slack, giving \(20+19=39\), not \(2t=40\).

Thus that profile admits a suitable \(O\) with outside opposition \(20\), not \(40\). The \(40\) there appears only if one fixes on the singleton \(O=\{1\}\) and ignores the better pair.
