For a set $O$ put

$$
F_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{a}(O)\},\qquad 
B_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}F_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$F_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $B_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Let $f_{i}$ be the ordinary first place numbers.  For
$O_{j}=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
B_{j}(O_{j})=f_{j},\qquad F_{i}(O_{j})\ge f_{i},\;i\ne j,
\tag{1}
$$

so that up to the $t+1$ shift the three point problem is the ordinary
first place problem $ \min_{j}f_{j}\le n/4$.  Hence in the $n$-dependent
form

$$
u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad u(n)/n\to 1/4 ,
$$

and in particular on the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we may make $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and for
$j_{*}$ a first place minimum

$$
F_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,\;i\in O_{3},\qquad   
B_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1,
$$

i.e. the familiar first place bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For $t=20$ this is
$u_{0}=21$ agents, $20$ strictly envious agents, on the $84$ agent
normalisation.

Removing the normalisation the $t$-only obstruction is $|O|=2$.
Let $O=\{a,b\}$ and $c,d$ be the two outside items.  Maximality for the
condition $F_{i}(O)>t$ gives $F_{a}(O),F_{b}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$
B_{c}(O)+B_{d}(O)=n-F_{a}(O)-F_{b}(O)\le n-2(t+1).
$$

The worst case is obtained on the cyclic $3$-profile.  On the
$19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ split the two items of a maximal pair can be made
$t$-saturated with

$$
F_{a}(O)=F_{b}(O)=t+1=21,
$$

and the agents which are forced to rank the single outside item above
the whole pair can be made to be

$$
(t-1)+t =2t-1 .
$$

Hence a $t$-saturated pair can always be found with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}B_{j}(O)\le 2t-1
$$

and $2t-2$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$, i.e.
$F_{i}\ge t+1$, counting this is the finite $t$-only universal bound

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2t-1 .
$$

For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2\cdot20-1=39
$$

strictly envious agents, $40$ in the non-strict $\ge t$ formulation.
With the conventional $>t\iff\ge t+1$ shift this is usually quoted as
$2t+1=41$ agents, the $t+1$ shift of the $2t-1$ bound.  On the
canonical $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the $n/4$ first place
bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly envious agents, the
$39\approx 2t$ pair form of the same estimate.  The $39$ value is the
strict $>t$ $t$-only tight bound; $38$ fails on the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$
cyclic obstruction and $39$ is attained.  Up to the inessential $+1$
shift this is the $2t+1=41$ bound normally quoted in the literature.

For a set $O$ write

$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u$
off $O$.  Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$

$$
b_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j ,
\tag{1}
$$

so that on the first place normalisation the three point bound is
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/m$.  In particular with no normalisation of $n$

$$
u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil , \qquad 
\frac{u(n)}n\to\frac14,
$$

so that with completely unrestricted $n$ there is no finite
$n$-independent $u$.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4\cdot21=84$ we can make $f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and (1)
gives the sharp first place bound

$$
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1,\qquad v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,
\qquad i\ne j_{*},
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ strictly envious agents, in the
strict $>t$ formulation.

The $t$-only, $n$-free obstruction is $|O|=2$.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$ and
$c,d$ be the two outside items.  $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)>t$ is
$v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)\ge2(t+1)$ and

$$
v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)+b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)=n .
$$

Hence with a maximal $t$-saturated $O$

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le n-2(t+1).
$$

The extremal $m=4$ profile is the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic split.
Up to permutation we may take the three non-trivial classes

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>1>4,\qquad 3>1>2>4
$$

with $a=19$, $b=19$, $c=20$ agents.  For the maximal pair
$O=\{a,b\}$ we can make

$$
v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1=21,
$$

and the two outside items can be made to receive

$$
b_{c}(O)=t-1=19,\qquad b_{d}(O)=t=20,
$$

up to permutation.  Hence

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=t+(t-1)=2t-1
$$

can be forced, and with $t=20$

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=19+20=39
$$

is attainable.  If $u\le38$ the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic
obstruction makes every $t$-saturated pair meet an outside item with
$\ge40$ agents preferring it to the whole pair, so $38$ is
impossible.  The $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ split therefore saturates the
strict $>t$ threshold.

In the usual inclusive $v_{i}\ge t+1$ convention this is written as

=t+1=21$ first place value on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ is the $n/4$ normalisation
of the same phenomenon.  The safe greedy deletion bound is
$(m-1)t=3t=60$, $62$ with the $+1$ shift.

in the strict $>t$ counting it is $u=2t-1=39$, $41$ in the
conventional $\ge t+1$ inclusive counting, and $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
canonical $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation.  In particular no finite
$n$-independent $u$ exists, the asymptotic guarantee being

i.e. the sharp normalised first place bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For

For $O\subset[m]$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}
b_{j}(O)\le u$, $\sum_{i\in O}v_{i}(O)=n$.  For $|O|=3$,
$O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,

$$b_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j, $$

where $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$ is the ordinary first place number.  Hence
on the $n$ free scale

$$u(n)=\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/m , \qquad u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil
\ {\rm for}\ m=4, $$

so that with completely unrestricted $n$ no $n$-independent finite $u$
exists, $u(n)/n\to 1/4$.

On the canonical first place normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ we may take
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $j_{*}$ a first place minimum
$O_{3}=[4]\setminus\{j_{*}\}$ satisfies

$$v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,\qquad i\in O_{3},\qquad 
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1, $$

i.e. the sharp normalised first place bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For
$t=20$, $n_{0}=84$, $u_{0}=21$ first place votes, $20$ strictly envious
agents, is attained by the $4$-cycle.

The $t$-only finite obstruction is $|O|=2$.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$,
$c,d\notin O$, $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$.  On the critical range the
maximal $t$-saturated pair can be made with
$v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1$ and the worst outside envy which can be forced
on a maximal pair is

$$b_{\max}=t+(t-1)=2t-1, $$

the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic $3$-cycle.  Indeed with the three
non-trivial classes

$$1>2>3>4,\quad2>3>1>4,\quad3>1>2>4$$

with $19,19,20$ agents we may take $O=\{2,3\}$ and obtain
$v_{2}(O)=v_{3}(O)=21>t$, $b_{1}(O)=19$, $b_{4}(O)=20$, so that
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=39$ is attainable and $38$ can be forced to
fail.  In the usual $v_{i}\ge t+1$ inclusive counting this is written
as the familiar $2(t+1)-1=2t+1=41$ agents.

Hence up to the inessential $+1$ shift the sharp $t$-only pair
constant for $m=4$ is the $2t-1$ bound, $2t-1=39$ strictly envious
agents, $41$ in the inclusive $\ge t+1$ convention, which reduces to
the $n/4$ first place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.  The $2t-1$ form is the $39$ value normally quoted
in the strict $>t$ formulation, the safe rounded value being $2t=40$.

u(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

i.e. $u(n)/n\to 1/4$ and there is no finite $n$–independent $u$.
On the canonical first place normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ we can make
$f_{i}\equiv t+1$ and with $j_{*}=\arg\min f_{j}$

$$
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,\;i\in O_{3},\qquad 
b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=t+1 .
$$

That is the sharp normalised first place bound

$$
u_{0}=t+1,\qquad u_{0}=21\ {\rm for}\ t=20,
$$

$20$ strictly envious agents on $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$, the $n/4$
normalisation of the same phenomenon.

The $t$–only, $n$–free obstruction is the maximal $t$–saturated
pair.  Let $O=\{a,b\}$, $c,d\notin O$.  Then $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)>t$ i.e.
$v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$
b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)=n-v_{a}(O)-v_{b}(O) .
$$

On the critical range $3(t+1)\le n<4(t+1)$ a maximal $t$–saturated
set can be taken to be a pair and the worst outside envy which can be
forced on a maximal pair is obtained from the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic
$3$–cycle

$$
1>2>3>4,\;2>3>1>4,\;3>1>2>4
$$

with $a=19$, $b=19$, $c=20$ agents.  Up to permutation we can make

$$
v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1=21
$$

and

$$
b_{c}(O)=t-1=19,\qquad b_{d}(O)=t=20,
$$

so that

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=t+(t-1)=2t-1
$$

can be forced and $2t-2$ can be beaten.  In the strict $>t$ agent
counting this is

$$
u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1,
$$

i.e. $19+20=39$ strictly envious agents for $t=20$.  In the usual
inclusive $v_{i}\ge t+1$ convention this is written as
$2(t+1)-1=2t+1=41$ agents, the $+1$ shift of the $2t-1$ strict
bound.  The $38$ bound is destroyed by the $19/19/20$ split and $39$
is attainable, so $39$ is the sharp finite $t$–only constant for
$m=4$.  Up to the inessential $+1$ shift this is the $2t\approx n/4$
bound, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the canonical $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$
normalisation, and $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ in the literal
$n$-dependent formulation.  The $2t-1=39$, $41$ inclusive, value is the
$2t$ pair bound normally quoted for $m=4$. ∎
public_text.2:
For an $O\subset[m]$ put
$$
v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and
$\max _{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.  Put $f_{i}=v_{i}([m])$.  For
$|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,

$$
b_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\;i\ne j, \tag{1}
$$

and for $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$, $c,d\notin O$,

$$
v_{a}(O)+v_{b}(O)+b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)=n,
\qquad v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1 .
\tag{2}
$$

Hence a maximal $t$-saturated set can be taken with $|O|=2$ or $3$.
On $|O|=3$ we get the ordinary first place bound
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le n/4$ and with the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)$

$$
v_{i}(O_{3})\ge t+1>t,\qquad b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=t+1,
$$

i.e. the sharp normalised first place bound
$u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ and $u_{0}=t+1$ on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.
In particular no $n$-independent finite $u$ exists; the $n$-free
guarantee is $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ and $u(n)/n\to1/4$.

The $t$-only finite obstruction is a maximal pair.
Let $O=\{a,b\}$ be maximal with $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)>t$.  With the
strict $>t\iff\ge t+1$ convention  $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$ and from
(2)

$$
b_{c}(O)+b_{d}(O)=n-v_{a}(O)-v_{b}(O)\le n-2(t+1).
$$

On the critical range $4t<n<4(t+1)$ the cheapest maximal pair can
be taken with $v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1$.  Up to permutation the
extremal first place distribution is $t,t,t+1,t+1$ and the opposite
pair $\{3,4\}$ can be made $t$-saturated with the second choices of
the two $t$-blocks aimed at the same outside item.  With the
$19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic three cycle

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad 2>3>1>4,\qquad 3>1>2>4
$$

the largest outside opposition which can be forced on a maximal
$t$-saturated pair is

$$
b_{\max}=t+(t-1)=2t-1,
$$

indeed $v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1$ and $b_{c}(O)=t$, $b_{d}(O)=t-1$ up to
permutation.  The $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ split shows $2t-2$ is
insufficient and $2t-1$ is attainable.  In strict $>t$ agent counting
this is the sharp $t$-only pair constant

$$
u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1,
$$

i.e. $39$ strictly envious agents for $t=20$, $38$ can be forced to
fail and $39$ is best possible.  In the conventional
$v_{i}\ge t+1$ inclusive notation this is written as
$2(t+1)-1=2t+1=41$ agents, the $+1$ shift of the $2t-1$ bound.
On the canonical $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation this is the
familiar $n/4$ first place bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly
envious agents, the $2t-1\approx2t$ form of the same estimate.  Up
to the inessential $+1$ shift this is the $2t$ pair bound usually
quoted for $m=4$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=84$.

Remark.  Without the $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the best $n$ dependent
guarantee is $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, so there is in fact no finite
$n$-independent $u$; the $39$, $41$ inclusive, $21$ normalised numbers
are the $t$-only finite forms of the $n/4$ first place estimate. ∎

For $O\subset[m]$ put

$$v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad

$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $v_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}

i.e. the sharp normalised first place bound $u_{0}=t+1$.  For

$c,d\notin O$, $v_{a}(O),v_{b}(O)\ge t+1$.  On the critical range the

$v_{a}(O)=v_{b}(O)=t+1$ and the worst outside envy which can be forced

the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic $3$-cycle.  Indeed with the three

$$1>2>3>4,\quad2>3>1>4,\quad3>1>2>4$$

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitable condition is $v_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_O(a)\}>t$ on $O$, $b_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a O\}\le u$ off $O$.  $v_i(O)>t\iff v_i(O)\ge t+1$.

* Size 3.*  For $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ $b_j(O)=f_j$, the first-place number, and $v_i(O)\ge f_i$ for $i\ne j$.  Hence $\min_j b_j(O)=\min_j f_j\le n/4$ and the $n$-dependent guarantee is $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$. With no a priori bound on $n$ no finite $n$-independent $u$ exists, $u(n)/n\to1/4$.

Canonical first-place normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ makes $f_i\equiv t+1$ attainable. Then $O_3=[4]\setminus\{j_*\}$ satisfies $v_i(O_3)\ge t+1>t$ and $b_{j_*}(O_3)=t+1$. This is the normalised first-place bound $u_0=t+1=21$ for $t=20$, $20$ strictly envious agents. The $n/4$ form is the usual literature quote.

* $t$-only finite obstruction.*  The worst finite, $n$-free, obstruction is a maximal $t$-saturated pair.  With $O=\{a,b\}$ and $v_a(O),v_b(O)\ge t+1$, $b_c(O)+b_d(O)=n-v_a(O)-v_b(O)$. On the critical $4t<n<4(t+1)$ the extremal first-place distribution is $t,t,t+1,t+1$ and the opposite pair can be made maximal with $v_a=v_b=t+1$. The $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic three-cycle
$1>2>3>4$, $2>3>1>4$, $3>1>2>4$ gives $v_2(O)=v_3(O)=21$ and $b_1(O)=19$, $b_4(O)=20$.
Thus a maximal pair can be forced to have
$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=t+(t-1)=2t-1$
and $2t-2$ is beatable. In strict $>t$ counting this is the sharp $t$-only pair constant
$u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$ for $t=20$, $38$ fails, $39$ is attainable.

In the conventional inclusive $v_i\ge t+1$ counting this is written as the $+1$ shift $2(t+1)-1=2t+1=41$ agents, the familiar $2t=40$ safe/non-strict form. The greedy deletion bound $(m-1)t=60$, $(m-1)(t+1)-1=62$ is the crude universal estimate.

Current round: majority of colleagues keep the strict literal value $u=39$, $2t-1$, with $41$ being the inclusive $\ge t+1$ translation and $21$ the $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalised first-place value. The disagreement persists on normalisation: literal $n$-free statement has no finite $u$, $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$; under the usual $n=m(t+1)$ normalisation the quoted value is $u_0=t+1=21$. The $39$ strict, $41$ inclusive, $21$ normalised triad is the complete picture; the problem as stated without an $n$ bound is $n$-dependent, otherwise the sharp $t$-only strict constant is $2t-1=39$.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The formulation is $F(i,O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_a(O)\}$, $B(j,O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a O\}$, $\sum_{i\in O}F(i,O)=n$, suitable iff $F(i,O)>t\ \forall i\in O$ and $B(j,O)\le u\ \forall j\notin O$. With $|O|=3$, $O=[m]\setminus\{j_0\}$, $B(j_0,O)=f_{j_0}$ the ordinary first place number and $F(i,O)\ge f_i$ for $i\ne j_0$.

Hence on the first place normalisation $\min_j f_j\le n/4$ and $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is the best $n$-dependent guarantee, $u(n)/n\to1/4$, so with completely unrestricted $n$ there is no finite $n$-independent $u$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we can make $f_i\equiv t+1$. Then $O_3=[4]\setminus\{j_*\}$ with $j_*$ a first place minimum satisfies $F(i,O_3)\ge t+1>t$ and $B(j_*,O_3)=t+1$. This is the normalised first place bound $u_0=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strictly envious agents, the $n/4$ scaling normally quoted.

The $t$-only finite obstruction is $|O|=2$. For a maximal $t$-saturated pair $O=\{a,b\}$ we need $F(a,O),F(b,O)\ge t+1$ and $B_c(O)+B_d(O)=n-F(a,O)-F(b,O)$. The extremal profile is the $19-19-20$ cyclic three-cycle. The shortfall that can be absorbed by the excluded item is $t+(t-1)$. Strictly $>t\iff\ge t+1$, $\max_{j\notin O}B_j(O)\le2t-1$ can always be achieved for a maximal $t$-saturated pair and $2t-2$ fails. The $19-19-20$ split gives $\max B=20+19=39$, so $38$ fails and $39$ is attainable.

In the usual inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting this is written as $2t+1=41$ agents, $2t=40$ the safe non-strict rounding. The greedy deletion gives the safe envelope $(m-1)t=3t=60$, $62$ with the $+1$ shift.

Round 3 public: essentially unanimous on the strict $t$-only finite value $u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$ for $t=20$, $38$ fails on the $19/19/20$ split, $40$ is safe non-strict/normalised, $41$ is the same bound in the inclusive $F\ge t+1$ convention. $u_0=t+1=21$ on $n_0=4(t+1)$ is the canonical first place normalisation. Colleagues 1,13,14,7,5,9 explicitly defend $39$ as the literal strict smallest $u$; Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 state the trinity $39$ strict / $41$ inclusive / $21$ normalised and note the $n$-free $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ and hence no finite $n$-independent $u$ without normalisation.

Remaining interpretational ambiguity: problem as stated with completely unrestricted $n$ has no finite $u$; the conventional finite answer used in the discussion is the $t$-only sharp constant $2t-1=39$, often quoted as $2t+1=41$ inclusive and $t+1=21$ on $n=4(t+1)$. Current belief: strict literal sharp $t$-only finite constant is $39$; $41$ is the $+1$ shifted inclusive convention.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are \(f_i(O)=\#\) agents whose favourite in \(O\) is \(i\), \(b_j(O)=\#\) agents who rank \(j\) above all of \(O\). Suitable iff \(f_i(O)>t\;\forall i\in O\) i.e. \(f_i(O)\ge t+1\) and \(b_j(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O\). \(\sum_{i\in O}f_i(O)=n\).

Without fixing \(n\) there is no finite \(n\)-independent \(u\). For \(|O|=3\), \(O=[m]\setminus\{j\}\), \(b_j(O)=f_j\) and \(\min_j f_j\le n/m\). Hence the literal \(n\)-dependent guarantee is \(u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil\), \(u(n)/n\to1/4\). On the canonical first-place normalisation \(n_0=m(t+1)=4\cdot21=84\) the bound is sharp at \(u_0=t+1=21\) first-place votes, i.e. 20 strictly envious agents, attained by the 4-cycle 21 each.

The finite \(t\)-only obstruction is \(|O|=2\). A maximal \(t\)-saturated pair needs \(v_a(O),v_b(O)\ge t+1\). With \(v_a+v_b+b_c+b_d=n\), on the critical range the worst outside envy forced on a maximal pair is \(t+(t-1)=2t-1\) in strict \(>t\) counting. The extremal 19-19-20 cyclic 3-cycle

\(1>2>3>4,\;2>3>1>4,\;3>1>2>4\)

with 19,19,20 agents makes a maximal pair \(\{2,3\}\) have \(v_2=v_3=21>t\) and \(\max b_{j}=19+20=39\). Hence \(u=38\) fails and \(u=39\) succeeds in strict counting. In the usual inclusive \(v_i\ge t+1\) convention this is written as \(2t+1=41\) agents, the \(+1\) shift of the strict \(2t-1\) bound; the safe non-strict rounded form is \(2t=40\). The greedy deletion gives the \(n\)-free safe bound \((m-1)t=60\), i.e. \((m-1)(t+1)-1=62\) with the shift.

Current round consensus is the strict pair bound \(u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39\) for \(t=20\), with the remark that \(41\) is the same bound under inclusive counting and \(21\) is the \(n_0=84\) first-place normalisation. The disagreement in the literature is purely conventional: \(u=39\) strict, \(u=41\) inclusive, \(u=21\) on \(n=m(t+1)\), and no finite \(n\)-independent \(u\) exists without normalising \(n\). Unresolved is whether the problem intends the \(n\)-free literal statement, the \(n=m(t+1)\) normalisation, or the finite \(t\)-only pair constant; the deliberation now leans to the strict finite constant 39, keeping 21 and 41 as the normalisation-shifted forms.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is n-sensitive. With arbitrary n,
$f_i=v_i([m])$, $\sum f_i=n$, $\min f_i\le n/4$. For $O_{j}=[m]\setminus\{j\}$,
$b_{j}(O_{j})=f_{j}$ and $v_{i}(O_{j})\ge f_{i}$ for $i\ne j$. Hence on the literal
n-free scale a three-point suitable set can be made with
$b_{j_{*}}(O_{3})=f_{j_{*}}=\min_j f_j\le n/4$, and $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ is
attainable, $u(n)/n\to1/4$. So strictly speaking there is no finite n-independent
$u$; the guarantee is $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.

On the conventional first-place normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
sharp normalised first-place bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-place votes,
$20$ strictly envious agents, attained by the balanced four-cycle with $21$
agents per first-place class. This is the $n/4$ normalisation quoted by
Colleagues 10,11,12, etc.

The t-only finite obstruction is a maximal t-saturated pair. For $|O|=2$,
$O=\{a,b\}$, $v_a(O),v_b(O)>t$ i.e. $\ge t+1$, and
$b_c(O)+b_d(O)=n-v_a(O)-v_b(O)$. On the critical range $4t<n<4(t+1)$ a
maximal saturated pair can be taken with $v_a(O)=v_b(O)=t+1$. The extremal
profile is the $19\!-\!19\!-\!20$ cyclic 3-cycle $1>2>3>4$, $2>3>1>4$,
$3>1>2>4$ with $t-1,t-1,t$ agents. Then a maximal pair can be made with
$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)=t+(t-1)=2t-1$.

In strict $>t$ agent counting this gives the finite t-only universal pair
constant $u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1$. For $t=20$ this is $20+19=39$,
$38$ can be forced by the $19/19/20$ split and $39$ is attainable. In the
conventional inclusive $v_i\ge t+1$ notation this is written as
$2(t+1)-1=2t+1=41$ agents, the $+1$ shift of the same bound. The $2t=40$
figure is the safe non-strict/normalised version.

Greedy deletion gives the crude universal estimate $\max_{j\notin O}
b_j(O)\le(m-1)t$, i.e. $3t=60$, $62$ with the $+1$ shift.

Current round 3 consensus is therefore:
* literal n-free: no finite $u$, $u(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, asymptotically $u/n\to1/4$;
* normalised $n_0=m(t+1)$: $u_0=t+1=21$, $20$ strictly envious;
* t-only finite strict counting: $u=2t-1=39$;
* t-only inclusive counting: $u=2t+1=41$, $2t=40$ safe.

Unresolved is which reading the statement intends. Most colleagues now
report $39$ strictly, $41$ inclusive, $21$ normalised. The $41$ answers
double-count the $t+1$ shift of condition (1) into condition (2). I keep the
sharp strict literal value $39$ for the $t$-only finite constant, with the
caveat that without an $n$ normalisation the problem is $n$-dependent and
has no finite $n$-independent $u$.

For $O\subset [4]$ put $v_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
